3. Noise Levels: See discussion of Impact of Downtown Expressway, Chapter II, Section A, Item 8.
4. Land:
a. The topography of the Randolph Project exhibits very little change and could be considered generally level. No natural hazards from unstable soil conditions are known to exist. As previously noted, the Randolph Area is currently predominantly urban residential in character.
b. Clearing and grading of land now covered with blighted housing units will result in minimal changes to the land and offer very little chance for a significant amount of soil erosion.
5. Vegetation and Wildlife:
a. No significant vegetation, with the exception of street trees, will be affected. Street trees in the clearance area will be preserved wherever possible. Several factors must be considered in saving the existing trees: 
(1) Location  the first factor to the considered; realignment and widening of streets and alleys will undoubtably take a toll of the existing trees.
(2) Maturity and Condition  old and diseased trees will be removed.
(3) Size  small caliper trees present no problems in removal or replacement.
(4) Specie and Habit of Growth  a tree desirable under one set of conditions can be a problem in another situation.
(5) Ease of Replacement  well established and thriving trees should be retained whenever possible.
